body_markdown:
All our cars have one thing in common: They are declining. Sometimes the decline happens quickly (think: brake line failure or overheating). Other times, it’s slower and harder to see—a pinhole of rust quietly bubbling up under your paint. The only recourse is to become a committed maintainer. Here’s some of our best advice for how (and why) to get started and how to keep going.


## 1. You Must Read *Maintenance: Of Everything*


To the layperson, maintenance is a prosaic chore, the sort of thing you pay not to do. Readers of this site and HDC magazine already know better. The simple joys and profound benefits of working on your own stuff have been the subject of several books covered in these pages, from the influential (if at times inscrutable) *[Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorcycles/the-never-ending-quest-for-zen/)* (reviewed in the November/December 2024 issue of *[Drivers Club](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine/)* ) and the hippy-culture-inflected *[How to Keep Your Volkswagen Alive](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B09QXQP4S2?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback)* to the more recent and excellent *[Shop Class as Soulcraft](https://www.thenewatlantis.com/publications/shop-class-as-soulcraft)* (by Matthew B. Crawford, a frequent HDC contributor). Even the fully initiated could reasonably wonder what else there could be left to say about the subject. The answer, in Stewart Brand’s opinion, is Everything.


Stripe Press


Although the book, *[Maintenance: Of Everything](https://stripe.press/book/maintenance-part-one)* , is a new addition to the canon, Brand is hardly a newcomer to the subject. From the late 1960s to the early 1980s, he published the *Whole Earth Catalog* , a wide-reaching, illustrated how-to guide that helped motivate legions of techies and DIYers (Apple founder Steve Jobs later called it “one of the bibles of my generation”).


His latest work, as its title implies, aims at a similar level of comprehensiveness. Brand looks at how maintenance plays out in everything from wooden sailboats and rifles to childbirth and laparoscopic surgery. He also reviews, with thoroughness and deep reverence, existing literature on the subject going back to the 17th century.


The various chapters and subheadings can seem disconnected (one digression, 15 pages long, deals with various forms of corrosion, which itself digresses into a detailed account of repairs effected to the Statue of Liberty). Yet Brand threads them together into a perspective on maintenance that subtly cuts against conventional wisdom.


For one thing, he’s an unabashed lover of tech. A lot of committed maintainers tend to have an ambivalence toward modernity—the sense that technology, in the name of convenience and profit, is pulling people further from the ability to understand and interact with our world. You’d expect Brand, who’s 88 years old, to have a similar sense of nostalgia. Instead, he earnestly declares, “[YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/Hagerty) is a damn miracle.”


Mario Hernandez


He’s not blind to the costs of modernity—he devotes an entire chapter to the decline of the internal combustion engine and its costs. Yet even here he adds that he was an early buyer of the Tesla Model S. More pointedly, he warns that “suicidal pessimism about civilization” has its own costs.


The reference to “civilization” isn’t incidental. Books about maintenance and DIY typically focus on individuals, on working in solitude to perfect a machine and oneself. There are such lone rangers in *Maintenance: Of Everything* —the book opens with tales of solo quests to sail around the globe (the winner, no surprise, was not the fastest boat but the one best maintained). Yet Brand is most engaging when he zooms out to look at how maintenance plays out at the corporate, societal, and even global historical levels.


Consider Brand’s comparison of the Rolls-Royce Silver Ghost to the Ford Model T. The former was a car created by the finest craftspeople in Britain with the intention of requiring little in the way of maintenance. The seemingly humbler Model T, in Brand’s telling, was a vehicle created in order to be maintainable, an engineering challenge that required extraordinarily precise manufacturing to ensure parts interchangeability.


Then Brand looks backward—all the way to the American Revolutionary War—arguing that it was the fledgling War Department’s embrace of standardized guns with interchangeable parts and subsequent investment in the required factories and tooling that enabled Henry Ford, more than a century later, to apply a similar approach to car making. Brand contrasts that with France’s revolutionaries, who squashed similar advances in French gun-making out of fear they would put traditional artisans out of business and subsequently industrialized later than other Western powers. Civilization, Brand thinks, is best off when the masses are invited to participate in its maintenance. He took his own advice while writing this book—you can find drafts online, where Brand welcomed comments from the public, many of which are included as footnotes in the printed publication.


If all this sounds, well, heavy, truly it’s not. *Maintenance: Of Everything* flows less like a PhD thesis than conversation over drinks with an extremely wise old friend. There are also, nestled within various anecdotes, great maintenance tips: Pay extra for stainless steel when possible, to avoid corrosion; the McMaster-Carr online catalog is a great resource for hard-to-find parts; novel isn’t always better because “Old systems break in familiar ways. New systems break in unexpected ways.” And, above all, keep an open mind. Chasing oil-leak issues recently, I recalled Brand’s quote from one of the sailboat captains who ruminated on a particular problem for two nights before pulling out any tools. “I did not want to crystallize my thinking prematurely,” he said. *–[David Zenlea](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/david-zenlea/)*


## 2. Treat Your Car Like You *Don’t* Own It


An insidious aspect of classic car ownership is that we often don’t drive them frequently enough to notice deterioration in certain systems. The brakes feel roughly the same this May as last, and so forth, so you never have reason to go through them until, one spring morning, you press on the pedal and wonder, “Were they always this bad?”


Fight entropy by inspecting your car as if you were about to purchase it. If you wouldn’t buy your own car, you probably shouldn’t drive your own car. Here are basic pre-purchase inspection items to get you started. Take detailed notes each year to keep track of issues as they arise.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


**Steering:** The steering wheel should have minimal play. Check for leaks, cracked bushings, and dust caps. Grab and shake various parts; there should be no detecable slop or motion.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


**Brakes:** The “hard, harder” test is a great place to start. While parked, press the brake pedal with the normal force to stop the car in traffic and hold that pressure. Now push even harder on the pedal as if doing a panic stop and hold for a couple of counts. The pedal should not sink or lose pressure during this simple test. If it does, you have issues that need to be dealt with. While driving, lightly apply the brakes. The car should stop straight. Drum brakes require more adjustment and maintenance to stop reliably and consistently.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


**Rubber Hoses:** Inspect them for cracking, and then give each a squeeze. If any are pillowy soft or rock hard, replace them.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


**Wiring:** While there often is not much to visually inspect with wiring, looking under the dashboard and around the chassis of the car is an easy way to spot chafing wires or corroded grounds before they show other symptoms. Also take the time to turn everything on and cycle it. Even electric things don’t like to sit and it’s best to find out if something is going to blow a fuse while in the driveway. Final check is, of course, a full light inspection for proper function.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


**Tires:** Date codes will likely make the call on many aging sets pretty easy, but even if the rubber is still young, you’re not in the clear yet. Look for debris wedged in the tire, proper inflation and tread depth, and that the rubber has no checking or visible flaws.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


**Drivetrain:** Check that the engine runs smoothly and has all the appropriate fluids topped up and in good condition. Inspect for leaks or loose parts under the car, looking at the transmission and differential as well. Rattles, squeaks, or other noises should be noted, at least; better yet, diagnosed and repaired. *–[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)*


## 3. Sometimes It’s Best to See a Professional


Maintenance is a great way for a DIY-er to commune with a beloved car—we all know how to change a wiper blade and check the oil level, right? That said, take your car to a pro every once in a while, even for seemingly small stuff. You’re after a few things: The first is to gauge the expertise and competence of any given shop. If they spill oil all over the valve covers, never go back. Once you find a good establishment, it’s wise to have them do some other maintenance—in this case, maintain a relationship with a valued partner who helps keep your car on the road. We all know good shops are hard to find.


Cameron Neveu


The last reason is particularly valuable: The right pro is an objective and knowledgeable second opinion about the health of your car. Many things do degrade slowly over time, and the owner might not notice (see: point 2). A marque expert is also an invaluable guide to explain how a particular model should feel. Is that steering slop normal or is something worn out? The right pro will know. *–[Larry Webster](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/lwebsterhagerty-com/)*


## 4. There Is Such a Thing as Too Much


A former colleague of mine, Mike Miller (now sadly gone), became known for his “Lifetime BMW Maintenance Schedule.” I used to joke with him, “Maintenance? What is that? When things break, you fix them, spending as little money as possible.” To a relentlessly thrifty do-it-yourselfer like me, the difference between “maintenance” and “repairs” is that if a car is broken, it needs to be repaired, whereas it never truly “needs” maintenance.


I’m mostly kidding, yet I am of the school of thought that trying to make an old car feel like a new one is a recipe for financial drain and disappointment, so I try to be practical about maintenance. The most visceral way to think of maintenance is in terms of its role in avoiding hard and soft failures. Hard failures are things that break and stop the car immediately.


Mario Hernandez


Soft failures gradually get worse but give you lots of warning before going over the edge. For example, you don’t need to interrupt a trip and head for the nearest dealership to change the brake pads the moment the warning light from the wear sensor comes on, but continuing to ignore it risks unsafe braking as well as damaging the rotors. Never changing the oil is the ultimate soft failure, as doing so will dramatically shorten engine lifetime, but will have no effect in weeks or months.


Probably the biggest potential hard failure a car can have is if it has an “interference” engine where valves and pistons move in and out of the same space, and a timing belt (and many do). If so, you’d be an idiot not to change the belt at its recommended service interval, because if it breaks, it causes the pistons to crash into the valves without warning, ruining your engine. Ball joints are another potentially catastrophic hard failure, as letting one go can cause you to lose control of the car, so any metallic clunking in the front end requires prompt attention.


Overheating can be a hard or a soft failure. A hard cooling failure comes from a leak, a broken fan belt, or anything else that causes the engine to suddenly overheat. Stopping the car immediately may save you thousands of dollars. In contrast, a soft failure occurs when high temperatures and insufficient airflow gradually send the gauge into the danger zone. As both of these risk warping or cracking the head, any hint of cooling system malfunction should be addressed immediately.


Zach Bowman


People love to talk about replacing “the bushings” as part of maintenance. (The ones they usually mean are in the front suspension or steering that can make the car feel wandery or clunky, but the ones on the alternator that keep the fan belt tight are important, too.) By all means, examine the car’s front end and replace anything that shows play (ideally in pairs, left and right), and flag anything with a torn rubber boot for replacement, as dirt and moisture will surely get in and hasten failure. But balance “do it all, do it once” with the knowledge that the quality of new parts is spotty, and you can easily replace something good with something worse.


There are also the little things that drive us nuts, which are very personal. I’m not sure whether compounding out a scratch or fixing a rattling glovebox qualifies as “maintenance.” Like many people, I’m especially sensitive to things that I touch, so easy-to-replace worn-out shift linkage bushings drive me crazy, and any play in the steering column itself is far more important to me than, say, old rear subframe bushings that clunk a bit over potholes.


Think of maintenance as a goalpost. The left post is a barn find or ran-when-parked car that has had nothing done for it for so long that it now needs a full back-to-front sort-out of everything. The right post is a pampered example with eye-poppingly expensive service records that brings all the money on an auction site.


My advice? Try to kick the football somewhere between the two. *–[Rob Siegel](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rsiegel/)*


## 5. To Maintain Your Car Properly You Must Maintain Yourself


Cameron Neveu


After spending 20 years on a waitlist, a fellow I know finally got the nod to move his four project cars and three project airplanes into a larger hangar at a local airport near Los Angeles. He is 75 and spends only about half the year in Southern California. It took him a month to move everything with rollbacks and forklifts.


Sometimes I marvel at people’s energy to keep a fleet of vintage vehicles running well into their golden years. But as I myself have aged, I’ve come to realize that some people seem rather, *ahem* , optimistic—either about how much they’ll get done with their remaining time or how much time they have remaining to get it all done. Working on, under, inside, behind the panels of, and up the small cavities of old cars is hard on the body at any age, but more so as we get older. And unless you can afford a full-time mechanic, maintaining and repairing more than one or two old cars yourself can feel like punching at waves. It can seem like nothing ever gets done—or done fully and properly.


However, there are things we can do to make it easier to keep our cars running with less effort and strain. First, invest in a lift. On your 40th birthday, you officially became “too old for this s**t,” and especially working under a car perched only on jack stands. Raising a car up so you can sit or stand next to or underneath the thing you are repairing will greatly improve your productivity and extend your wrenching life.


Chris Stark


Cameron Neveu


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


Also, pay to climatize your garage. No matter where you live, it’s almost always too hot or too cold. Both conditions increase fatigue and increase the number of excuses we can invent to avoid doing necessary maintenance and repair. And while you’re at it, invest in good tools, the kind that are a pleasure to hold and work with, and organize them so they’re easy to find. The right tool gets jobs done quickly and efficiently and makes working on a car a satisfying pleasure. The wrong tool only produces frustration that exacerbates your wrinkles and high blood pressure.


Lastly, if your goal in your later years is to spend more time driving and less time wrenching, cut the number of cars you are responsible for. That can be like picking which child to sell, but the other kiddos will look and run better once your attention is less divided. After all, cars are not children. They are indifferent machines with lots of moving parts, all waiting for their moment to break. Sometimes, if you really love something, the best thing to do for it is to set it free. So it can break in someone else’s garage. *–[Aaron Robinson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/aaron-robinson/)*
